books.title: In the Mountains
books.art_why: The book shows real mountain animals that exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: The small striped chipmunk lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small chipmunk with dark stripes along its back stands on a rocky mountain ledge, tail raised, looking alert. Low green plants and pine trees grow around the rocks, with higher mountain slopes visible behind it.

pages.text: Yes, the small gray squirrel lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small gray squirrel clings to the trunk of a pine tree in the mountains, its bushy tail curled behind it. Rough bark, green needles and rocky ground below show the mountain forest where it lives.

pages.text: Yes, the small furry rabbit lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small furry rabbit sits in a mountain meadow among tufts of grass and scattered rocks. Its soft brown fur and long ears are clear as it looks across the open ground, with mountain slopes rising in the background.

pages.text: Yes, the small sly fox lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A small sly fox stands on a mountain path, reddish fur bright against gray rocks and low shrubs. Its narrow face is alert and its bushy tail trails behind as it watches from the edge of the trail.

pages.text: Yes, the big strong eagle lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big strong eagle soars above rocky mountain peaks, wide wings spread against the sky. Below are steep cliffs and distant ridges, showing the high mountain home where this powerful bird lives. Its sharp eyes look down over the landscape.

pages.text: Yes, the big proud deer lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big proud deer stands on a grassy mountain slope, head held high and antlers branching above it. Pine trees and rocky ridges rise behind the deer as it looks out over its mountain home.

pages.text: Yes, the big hungry bear lives in the mountains. Does anything else live in the mountains?
pages.brief: A big hungry bear walks through a mountain clearing, head low as it searches for food. Thick brown fur covers its heavy body, and rocks, grasses and pine trees surround the bear on the mountainside.

pages.text: Yes, many animals live in the mountains. Can you name these animals that live in the mountains?
pages.brief: Many mountain animals appear together across a rocky mountain landscape: a striped chipmunk, a gray squirrel, a furry rabbit, a sly fox, a strong eagle, a proud deer and a hungry bear. They stand among rocks, grasses and pine trees under open sky.

books.title: Animals, Animals
books.art_why: The book presents real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. Elk run fast. Elk live in the mountains.
pages.brief: Elk are shown running fast in a mountain setting, with more than one elk moving across the slopes. The scene shows the animals in the mountains where elk live, matching the page’s simple statement about many kinds of animals and the speed and home of elk.

pages.text: Giraffes have spots. Giraffes are tall.
pages.brief: Giraffes are shown standing tall, with their spotted coats clearly visible. The scene focuses on the giraffes’ spots and height, showing the animals as tall creatures with spots, exactly as the page describes them. The brief scene keeps attention on these two features.

pages.text: Elephants are strong. Elephants have long trunks.
pages.brief: Elephants are shown as strong animals, with their long trunks visible. The scene centers on the elephants’ strength and their long trunks, presenting the animals simply and directly as the page describes them. No other details are needed.

pages.text: Camels can go without water for a long time. Camels live in deserts.
pages.brief: Camels are shown in a desert setting. The scene presents camels going without water for a long time and living in deserts, focusing on the animals themselves and the desert place where they live, just as the page states.

pages.text: Foxes have bushy tails. Foxes live in holes in the ground.
pages.brief: Foxes are shown with bushy tails, near holes in the ground. The scene shows the foxes’ bushy tails and the holes in the ground where foxes live, keeping the picture focused on the animals and their home as described on the page.

pages.text: Zebras live in grassy places. Zebras have stripes.
pages.brief: Zebras are shown with stripes in a grassy place. The scene shows zebras living in grassy places, with their stripes visible, focusing on the animals and the grassy setting where they live, just as the page describes.

pages.text: Hippos live near water. Hippos have almost no hair.
pages.brief: Hippos are shown near water. The scene shows hippos close to water, with their skin appearing to have almost no hair, focusing on the animals and the water nearby as the page describes them. The picture stays simple and direct.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. Polar bears eat seals. Polar bears live in cold places.
pages.brief: Polar bears are shown in a cold place. The scene shows polar bears eating seals and living in cold places, focusing on the animals and the cold setting where they live, just as the page states.

books.title: Let's Make Lemonade
books.art_why: Children making lemonade from real lemons, water and sugar is everyday real life that a camera can show.

pages.text: It’s so hot today. We’re so thirsty for a cold drink.
pages.brief: Two young children stand in a bright, sunny kitchen, faces flushed and fanning themselves with their hands, looking hot and thirsty. A warm sunlit window behind them shows a very hot day outside, and they look around hoping for something cold to drink.

pages.text: Let’s make a cold drink. Let’s make a sweet drink.
pages.brief: The two children stand together at the kitchen counter, talking and pointing at the cupboard and fridge as they plan a cold, sweet drink. One child holds an empty glass, the other has a hand out, ready to start gathering what they need.

pages.text: Let’s make lemonade. Let’s make it in this pitcher.
pages.brief: A clear pitcher stands on the kitchen counter beside a bowl of fresh yellow lemons. One child holds the pitcher steady with both hands while the other reaches for a lemon, ready to make lemonade in the pitcher.

pages.text: Add cold water. Add white sugar.
pages.brief: A child pours cold water from a jug into the pitcher, water splashing gently inside. Beside them, another child tips a spoon of white sugar into the pitcher, the sugar falling in a small white stream onto the water.

pages.text: Roll and cut the lemons. Squeeze the lemons.
pages.brief: Small hands roll lemons firmly back and forth on the wooden counter, then cut them into halves on a board. The children squeeze the lemon halves over the pitcher, juice dripping down into the water below.

pages.text: Spot the lemon seeds. Pick out all the seeds!
pages.brief: A child leans close over the cut lemons and the pitcher, eyes searching for pale lemon seeds. Fingers pick the seeds out one by one and set them aside on the counter, away from the drink.

pages.text: Stir the lemonade with a long spoon.
pages.brief: A child holds a long spoon and stirs the lemonade round and round inside the pitcher, sugar swirling and dissolving. The other child watches closely, hands on the counter, as the drink turns pale and cloudy yellow.

pages.text: Don’t spill the pitcher! Lemonade is sticky.
pages.brief: A child carries the full pitcher carefully with both hands, walking slowly and watching the lemonade inside so it does not slosh. The other child walks beside them with hands out, ready to help steady it.

pages.text: Our drink looks cold. Our drink looks sweet.
pages.brief: The pitcher of lemonade sits on the table with two glasses filled, the drink pale yellow and beaded with cold. The children look at the glasses, smiling, pleased that their drink looks cold and sweet.

pages.text: We’re so thirsty for our lemonade.
pages.brief: The two children sit at the table holding their glasses of lemonade, drinking big gulps with happy faces. The pitcher stands between them, and they look refreshed after being so thirsty on a hot day.

books.title: All Kinds of Factories
books.art_why: Factories, machines and the goods they make all exist today, so real photographs fit.

pages.text: What Is a Factory? Factories are big buildings where goods are made.
pages.brief: A very large factory building seen from outside, wide and long with a tall roof, standing open to show goods being made inside it by workers at benches and machines.

pages.text: Some factories are in the city. Some factories are in the country.
pages.brief: Two views side by side: on one side a factory standing among busy city streets and tall buildings, on the other a factory standing in open countryside with fields and few buildings around it.

pages.text: Some factories use huge machines. Some factories use small machines.
pages.brief: Inside one factory, enormous heavy machines tower over the floor; inside another, small compact machines sit on workbenches, shown together so the big and small machines can be compared.

pages.text: Some factories have robots make goods. Some factories have people make goods. Some factories have both make goods.
pages.brief: Three factory floors shown: one where robot arms work alone making goods, one where people work with their hands making goods, and one where robots and people work together on the same line.

pages.text: What Do Factories Make? This factory turns wood into paper. People write or draw on paper.
pages.brief: Inside a paper factory, stacked logs of wood go into a machine and come out as flat sheets of paper; nearby, hands hold a sheet of paper and a pencil draws on it.

pages.text: This factory turns cotton into cloth. People use cloth to make clothes.
pages.brief: In a cloth factory, fluffy white cotton bolls are fed into machines that spin and weave it into long rolls of cloth; finished cloth is then cut and sewn into clothes.

pages.text: This factory turns sand into glass. People use glass in windows.
pages.brief: At a glass factory, piles of pale sand are heated in a furnace and turned into flat sheets of glass, which are then fitted into the frame of a window on a building.

pages.text: This factory puts parts together to make cars. People use cars to drive to different places.
pages.brief: On a car factory line, metal parts and panels are fitted and joined together into a finished car; the finished car is then shown on a road driving people to different places.

pages.text: What did you use today that came from a factory?
pages.brief: A child sits at a table at home, looking thoughtfully at everyday objects laid out in front of them, things that were made in factories and used during the day.

books.title: What's In That Pouch?
books.art_why: Koalas, wallabies, bilbies and kangaroos are real animals living today, so real photographs suit this book.

pages.text: Some animal moms carry the baby in a pouch. The baby rides and sleeps in the pouch.
pages.brief: A mother animal resting in a leafy spot with her small baby tucked inside the pouch on her belly. The baby's head and tiny paws poke out as it rides along, then settles down to sleep curled inside the warm pouch.

pages.text: It’s a baby koala! (koh-AW-luh) What’s in that pouch?
pages.brief: A fluffy baby koala peering out from the pouch on its mother's front as she clings to a tree trunk. The little koala's grey ears and dark nose show above the pouch opening while the mother holds on to the bark.

pages.text: A koala sits in trees. A koala eats leaves.
pages.brief: A koala sitting high in the fork of a gum tree, gripping the branches with strong claws. Its fluffy grey body is settled among green leaves, and it chews a mouthful of leaves pulled from a nearby stem.

pages.text: It’s a baby wallaby! What’s in that pouch?
pages.brief: A small baby wallaby looking out from the pouch on its mother's belly. The mother stands in low grass, her front paws held close, while the baby's head and ears show clearly at the pouch opening.

pages.text: A wallaby lives near the woods. A wallaby eats plants.
pages.brief: A wallaby standing at the edge of woodland, upright on its strong back legs with its tail resting on the ground behind it. It nibbles low green plants and grasses growing between the trees at the wood's edge.

pages.text: It’s two baby bilbies! What’s in that pouch?
pages.brief: Two tiny baby bilbies crowded together inside their mother's pouch, their long pointed snouts and thin ears close to the opening. The mother sits on sandy ground, her silky grey-brown fur lit by soft daylight.

pages.text: A bilby lives in the desert. A bilby eats bugs and seeds.
pages.brief: A bilby on dry desert sand, with reddish earth and sparse scrub around it. Its long snout digs at the ground where it finds insects, and small seeds lie scattered on the sand near its front paws.

pages.text: I’m a baby kangaroo! I’m in my mom’s pouch!
pages.brief: A baby kangaroo inside the pouch on its mother's belly, its head out and ears up, looking straight ahead. The mother stands in open ground, her big back legs planted and her long tail stretched behind her.

pages.text: A kangaroo hops in the bushes. A kangaroo eats plants.
pages.brief: A kangaroo hopping through low green bushes, powerful back legs pushing off the ground and tail balancing behind. Further along it stops, stands upright and nibbles the leaves and plants growing among the shrubs.

pages.text: Me! Me! Me! Me! Me! What’s in that pouch?
pages.brief: Several baby animals each pop their heads out of their mothers' pouches at once, little faces and ears appearing one after another in trees, grass and dry sand, all eager to be seen and counted.

books.title: The First Strawberry
books.art_why: A real, everyday gardening activity that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Do you love strawberries? Try growing your own!
pages.brief: A young child in a sunny garden holds a big ripe red strawberry in each hand, smiling. Around them, strawberry plants with green leaves and small red berries grow in a raised bed of dark soil, and a wooden basket of picked strawberries rests on the grass.

pages.text: Pick a sunny spot for your strawberry patch in spring.
pages.brief: A garden on a bright spring morning. A child walks across the lawn and stops beside an empty patch of bare soil, choosing the sunniest corner. Warm sunlight falls across the ground, with spring flowers and a garden shed in the background.

pages.text: Buy some plants for your strawberry patch.
pages.brief: At a garden centre, a child lifts a tray of small strawberry plants in little pots. The young green plants have fresh leaves and damp soil around their roots. Shelves of plants and stacked pots fill the background as the child carries the tray.

pages.text: Plant the plants in your strawberry patch. Leave room for them to spread.
pages.brief: In the sunny garden patch, a child kneels on the soil and presses a small strawberry plant into a hole, patting the earth around it. Several more plants sit in a row, spaced well apart with bare soil between them, room to spread.

pages.text: Spread straw in your strawberry patch. Straw helps prevent weeds and pests.
pages.brief: The child spreads handfuls of golden straw around the young strawberry plants, tucking it under the green leaves and over the bare soil. The straw covers the ground between the plants in a thick, soft layer, with a fork and a straw bale nearby.

pages.text: Water your strawberry patch at least twice a week.
pages.brief: The child stands beside the strawberry patch holding a watering can, tipping water gently over the plants and the straw. Droplets soak into the dark soil around each plant, and a second watering can waits on the path behind.

pages.text: The plants in your strawberry patch will bloom. Then, the plants will make small green fruits.
pages.brief: The strawberry plants in the patch are covered in small white flowers. Some flowers have dropped, and tiny green fruits hang where they were, tucked beneath green leaves. The child bends down close to look at the little green berries forming.

pages.text: The green fruits in your strawberry patch will turn pale. Then they will turn red.
pages.brief: Low to the ground, the small strawberries on the plants are changing colour. Some are still green, some are pale white-pink, and a few have turned bright red. The child crouches beside the patch, pointing at one red berry among the leaves and straw.

pages.text: Pick those fruits in your strawberry patch. Wash and eat them.
pages.brief: The child kneels in the patch and picks the ripe red strawberries, placing them into a small basket. Later, at a garden tap, the child rinses the berries under running water and pops one into their mouth.

pages.text: The first strawberry will taste the very best.
pages.brief: The child sits on the grass beside the strawberry patch, holding one perfect red strawberry up to the sunshine, eyes bright and a wide smile, ready to take the very first bite. The basket of strawberries rests beside them.

books.title: How Many Teeth?
books.art_why: All the animals are real and can be photographed today, so real photographs suit every page.

pages.text: Different animals have of teeth.
pages.brief: A group of very different animals — a small bird, a rabbit, a lizard and a dog — gather on short green grass in bright daylight, mouths open enough to show their teeth, making clear that different animals have different sets of teeth.

pages.text: A snake can have two fangs.
pages.brief: A close-up photograph of a snake's head with its mouth open wide, showing two sharp pointed fangs at the front of its jaw, taken outdoors against blurred green leaves and a thin brown branch in soft daylight.

pages.text: A vampire bat can have twenty teeth.
pages.brief: A vampire bat hangs upside down from a rough grey branch in a dark cave, its small face turned toward the camera with its mouth open, showing a row of tiny sharp teeth, lit by a single soft beam of light.

pages.text: A horse can have forty teeth.
pages.brief: A brown horse stands in a grassy meadow, its head turned to the side with its lips pulled back, showing a long row of large flat front teeth, its mane falling over its neck in warm afternoon sunlight.

pages.text: An opossum can have fifty teeth.
pages.brief: An opossum stands on a fallen log in a woodland at dusk, its pink nose lifted and its mouth open wide, showing many small pointed teeth, with dry leaves and dark tree trunks behind it.

pages.text: An alligator can have eighty teeth.
pages.brief: An alligator rests at the edge of a slow brown river, its long jaws open wide to show rows of sharp white teeth along both jaws, while green plants and still water fill the background in bright sun.

pages.text: A sand tiger shark can have ninety-six teeth.
pages.brief: A sand tiger shark swims close to the sandy sea floor in clear blue-green water, its mouth slightly open to show narrow pointed teeth, with small fish and rippled sand visible behind it.

pages.text: A dolphin can have two hundred fifty teeth.
pages.brief: A dolphin floats near the surface of bright blue sea water, its head turned toward the camera and its mouth open, showing a long row of small cone-shaped teeth along its jaw, sunlight rippling on the water.

pages.text: A snail can have teeth!
pages.brief: An extreme close-up of a garden snail on a wet green leaf, its small mouth pressed to the leaf as it feeds, its shell and two upper tentacles clear, with the rows of tiny teeth far too small to see.

pages.text: How many teeth do you have?
pages.brief: A young child about six years old stands in front of a bathroom mirror, smiling widely and pointing a finger at their own front teeth, the reflection showing an open grin, a toothbrush and cup on the sink beside them.

books.title: Arctic Animals
books.art_why: All the Arctic animals shown are real creatures living today, so real photographs work.

pages.text: Some animals live in cold places. The Arctic is one of the coldest places on Earth.
pages.brief: A wide icy Arctic landscape stretching to the horizon, with snow-covered ground, pale sky and cold blue light over frozen water, showing one of the coldest places on Earth where animals make their home.

pages.text: Hares live in the Arctic. They turn white in the winter.
pages.brief: An Arctic hare sitting on snowy ground, its coat white against the snow, long ears held up and dark eyes visible, blending into the winter landscape around it.

pages.text: Snowy owls live in the Arctic. They hunt in the day.
pages.brief: A snowy owl perched on a low snowy rise in daylight, white feathers with dark markings, yellow eyes scanning the bright Arctic ground as it looks for prey.

pages.text: Foxes live in the Arctic. They have thick fur.
pages.brief: An Arctic fox standing on snow in the open, its thick bushy fur and small rounded ears clear to see, cold wind ruffling the coat as it faces forward.

pages.text: Wolves live in the Arctic. They hunt in packs.
pages.brief: A pack of wolves moving together across snowy Arctic ground, several animals running close in a group, breath in the cold air, hunting as a team.

pages.text: Caribou live in the Arctic. They are good swimmers.
pages.brief: Caribou with large antlers wading through cold Arctic water, bodies partly submerged, heads above the surface as they swim across a river or lake.

pages.text: Moose live in the Arctic. They fight with their antlers.
pages.brief: Two moose standing face to face on snowy ground, heads lowered with big antlers pushed together as they fight, breath steaming in the cold Arctic air.

pages.text: Harp seals live in the Arctic. They have white fur as pups.
pages.brief: A harp seal pup with fluffy white fur lying on Arctic ice beside an adult seal, the pup resting near the edge of cold blue water.

pages.text: Orcas live in the Arctic. They hunt many sea animals.
pages.brief: An orca surfacing in cold Arctic water, tall black dorsal fin and white markings breaking the surface, dark sea around it as it hunts sea animals.

pages.text: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Moms stay with their cubs for years.
pages.brief: A mother polar bear standing on snowy Arctic ice with her cubs close beside her, the family together on the frozen ground near cold open water.

books.title: City Animals
books.art_why: All the animals and city places are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Many people live in cities. Many kinds of animals live in cities, too.
pages.brief: A busy city street with people walking along the sidewalk past buildings, and several kinds of city animals nearby among them, showing that many people and many animals share the same city places.

pages.text: They eat food people throw away. Mice live in cities.
pages.brief: Small mice on a city sidewalk and beside a rubbish area, nibbling at thrown-away food scraps lying on the ground, in the kind of paved city spot where people leave food behind.

pages.text: Geese and ducks live in cities. They swim in ponds in parks.
pages.brief: Geese and ducks on a park pond in a city park, swimming on the water with green grass and trees along the bank behind them.

pages.text: Squirrels make nests in trees. Squirrels live in cities.
pages.brief: A squirrel in a city tree, carrying nesting material and building its nest among the branches, with more city trees and buildings visible behind.

pages.text: Pigeons live in cities. Some people like to feed pigeons.
pages.brief: Pigeons gathered on the ground in a city, with people nearby holding out food and feeding the pigeons as the birds cluster around their hands and feet.

pages.text: They like to come out at night. Opossums live in cities.
pages.brief: Opossums out at night in a city, moving along in the dark near buildings and street edges, active while the city around them is quiet and shadowed.

pages.text: Hawks live in cities. They make nests on tall buildings.
pages.brief: A hawk perched at a nest built on a tall city building, with the high wall and ledges around it and the city roofline stretching behind.

pages.text: People bring them to the park. Dogs live in cities.
pages.brief: Dogs in a city park with people bringing them there, walking them on the grass and paths among trees, the dogs moving beside the people.

pages.text: Raccoons live in cities. They take food from trash bins.
pages.brief: Raccoons at a city trash bin, reaching in and pulling food out of the bin, with the paved street and building wall around them.

pages.text: What kinds of animals do you see? Do you see animals where you live?
pages.brief: A child in a city looking around at the animals nearby, watching the creatures that live on the same streets, with city buildings and outdoor space around.

books.title: Spending Dimes One at a Time
books.art_why: The book shows a real store, coins, and toys that exist today.

pages.text: At the store, a sign says that each item costs one dime. I have ten dimes. I spend one dime. Now the ball is mine.
pages.brief: At a store, a young child stands beside a display of small items. The child holds ten dimes, then sets one dime down and picks up a ball. The ball is now in the child’s hands. The other items wait on the display.

pages.text: How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: The same young child stands at the store display and looks at the dimes still in hand. The child counts the remaining dimes after buying the ball. The ball is held beside the dimes. The child’s face shows thinking about how many dimes are left.

pages.text: I have nine dimes. I spend one dime. Now the tiger is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds nine dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy tiger. The tiger is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have eight dimes. I spend one dime. Now the whistle is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds eight dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy whistle. The whistle is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have seven dimes. I spend one dime. Now the robot is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds seven dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy robot. The robot is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have six dimes. I spend one dime. Now the puppet is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds six dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy puppet. The puppet is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have five dimes. I spend one dime. Now the airplane is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds five dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy airplane. The airplane is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have four dimes. I spend one dime. Now the turtle is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds four dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a toy turtle. The turtle is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have three dimes. I spend one dime. Now the sticker is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds three dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a sticker. The sticker is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dimes and looks at them, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have two dimes. I spend one dime. Now the key chain is mine. How many dimes are left?
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds two dimes. The child sets one dime down and picks up a key chain. The key chain is now the child’s. The child still holds the remaining dime and looks at it, wondering how many are left.

pages.text: I have one dime. I spend one dime. Now the shell is mine. I have zero dimes, but I have ten items!
pages.brief: At the store, the child holds one dime. The child sets the last dime down and picks up a shell. The child now has zero dimes. Around the child are the ten items: ball, tiger, whistle, robot, puppet, airplane, turtle, sticker, key chain, and shell.

books.title: Caring For Earth
books.art_why: Gardens, trees, bikes, recycling bins and children helping outdoors all exist in the real world and can be photographed today.

pages.text: How can we help take care of Earth? We care for Earth when we tend gardens.
pages.brief: A sunny community garden with vegetable beds and flowers. Two children kneel beside a row of young plants, one loosening soil with a small trowel while the other tips a watering can. An adult gardener in gloves pulls weeds nearby, and wooden raised beds and a watering hose sit behind them.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we plant new trees.
pages.brief: Children planting young trees in a grassy schoolyard or park. One child holds a thin sapling upright inside a freshly dug hole while another shovels soil back in. A row of newly planted saplings with soft soil around their bases stretches across the grass behind them.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we reuse things.
pages.brief: A bright kitchen or classroom table where a child reuses everyday items instead of throwing them away. An old glass jar holds pencils and paintbrushes, a cloth bag is stuffed with shopping, and a refilled drink bottle stands beside a lunchbox. Shelves with reused boxes and containers sit behind.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we recycle.
pages.brief: A child sorting rubbish at a row of recycling bins in a school corridor or yard. The child drops an empty can into one bin while paper and a plastic bottle wait in a crate on the ground. The bins stand open with mixed clean materials inside.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we ride our bikes to school.
pages.brief: Children riding bicycles along a quiet street towards school, helmets on and backpacks bouncing. Two children pedal side by side while another child ahead rings a bell. In the background a school building and a rack of parked bikes wait by the gate.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we use less water.
pages.brief: A child at a bathroom sink turning the tap off tightly while brushing their teeth, a mug of water beside them. Through the open door a garden sprinkler is off and a watering can sits by potted plants. A small drip from the tap has stopped on the clean basin.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we save electricity.
pages.brief: A child switching off a light in a bright room, hand on the switch, while afternoon sunlight comes through the open curtains. A television and a lamp are turned off, and a plug is pulled out of the wall socket nearby. A parent smiles from the doorway.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we help animals.
pages.brief: Children helping animals in a garden or park. One child hangs a bird feeder filled with seed from a branch while another fills a shallow dish of water on the ground. A dog sits beside them, and small birds gather on a hedge behind.

pages.text: We care for Earth when we clean up trash outdoors.
pages.brief: Children wearing gloves and holding large bags, picking up litter in a park. One child bends to collect a paper wrapper from the grass while another carries a full bag. Trees, a bench and a grassy slope surround them in the sunshine.

pages.text: We can care for Earth in many different ways. Our care can make a big difference.
pages.brief: A cheerful group of children outdoors in a neighbourhood park, each busy with a different helpful job: one waters plants, one holds a full litter bag, one stands beside a bicycle, one fills a birdbath. Trees, garden beds and a bright sky fill the scene behind them.

books.title: Crazy Cakes
books.art_why: real decorated cakes and frosting can be photographed

pages.text: Some artists use paint or marble to make their art. Other artists use cake and frosting!
pages.brief: In a bright workspace, an artist’s hands decorate a cake with frosting beside art materials such as paint and smooth marble, showing that some artists make art with cake while others use paint or stone.

pages.text: Some of their cakes just look pretty. Other cakes look like something else.
pages.brief: On a display table in the picture, two decorated cakes are shown side by side: one cake with smooth frosting is simply pretty, while the other is shaped and decorated to look like something else entirely.

pages.text: This cake looks like a pretty peacock.
pages.brief: A whole cake made from cake and frosting is shaped and decorated to look like a pretty peacock, with a rounded body and a spread tail, sitting on display in the centre of the picture.

pages.text: This cake looks like a giant rooster.
pages.brief: A giant cake shaped and decorated to look like a giant rooster stands on display in the centre of the picture, with a rounded body, a head and a tail made from cake and frosting.

pages.text: This cake looks like a fancy crown.
pages.brief: A fancy crown cake made from cake and frosting is shaped and decorated to look like a royal crown, sitting on display in the centre of the picture with a rounded band and a high pointed top.

pages.text: This cake looks like a fish and hook.
pages.brief: A cake shaped and decorated to look like a fish and a hook sits on display in the centre of the picture, with the whole fish body and curved hook made from cake and frosting.

pages.text: This cake looks like a busy beehive.
pages.brief: A whole cake shaped and decorated to look like a busy beehive sits on display in the centre of the picture, with a rounded hive shape and fine busy details made from cake and frosting.

pages.text: This cake looks like a treasure chest.
pages.brief: A whole cake shaped and decorated to look like a treasure chest sits on display in the centre of the picture frame, with a chest shape and small treasure details made from cake and frosting.

pages.text: This cake looks like a magic unicorn.
pages.brief: A whole cake shaped and decorated to look like a magic unicorn sits on display in the centre of the picture, with a unicorn body and a single pointed horn made from cake and frosting.

pages.text: These cakes look almost too good to eat. They taste as good as they look!
pages.brief: A group of finished decorated cakes sits together on display in the final picture, each single one looking almost too good to eat, while their tasty appearance suggests they taste as good as they look.

books.title: Sew Who?
books.art_why: Craft materials, hands and sewing tools exist in the real world today.

pages.text: Are you ready to make an owl? Here is what you need to get started.
pages.brief: A table is set up for an owl sewing project, with the materials needed to get started laid out in an inviting craft space. The scene is ready for a child to begin making a felt owl, and the supplies wait to be picked up.

pages.text: Cut two body shapes from brown felt.
pages.brief: Hands use scissors to cut two owl body shapes from a sheet of brown felt on a work table. The two brown felt pieces lie side by side, shaped for the body of the owl project.

pages.text: Cut two eyes and one belly from white felt. Cut two wings and one beak from orange felt.
pages.brief: Hands cut two eye shapes and one belly shape from white felt, then cut two wing shapes and one beak shape from orange felt. The white and orange felt pieces are arranged on the table for the owl.

pages.text: Sew them in place. Pin the eyes on one of the body shapes.
pages.brief: Hands pin two white felt eyes onto one brown felt body shape on the work table, then sew the eye pieces in place with a needle and thread. The second brown body shape rests nearby.

pages.text: Pin the beak under the eyes. Sew it in place.
pages.brief: Hands pin the orange felt beak under the white felt eyes on the brown body shape, then sew the beak in place. The small orange beak sits centered below the eyes on the owl face.

pages.text: Sew it in place. Pin the belly under the beak.
pages.brief: Hands finish sewing the orange felt beak in place on the brown felt body, then pin the white felt belly under the beak. The belly piece is positioned on the front of the owl body.

pages.text: Pin the wings and sew them in place.
pages.brief: Hands pin the two orange felt wings to the sides of the brown felt body, then sew the wings in place with needle and thread. The owl shape begins to show its wings on the work table.

pages.text: Place stuffing inside. almost together. Pin and sew the two body shapes.
pages.brief: Hands push stuffing inside the brown felt owl body, bringing the two body shapes almost together. The edges are pinned and sewn as the stuffing fills the owl shape on the table.

pages.text: Sew the two body shapes all the way together.
pages.brief: Hands sew the two brown felt body shapes all the way together around the edge, closing the stuffed owl. The needle and thread move along the outer seam on the work table.

pages.text: Use markers to finish your owl.
pages.brief: Hands use markers to add finishing details to the finished felt owl on the work table. The markers draw features on the owl as the sewing project is completed, giving the owl its final look.

books.title: Which Tree?
books.art_why: Real trees and leaves exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: You can tell trees by their leaves.
pages.brief: A close view of several different tree leaves lying on mossy ground, each leaf a different shape and edge, with green trees standing behind them in a sunny woodland. The leaves are clear and separate, showing how one tree's leaves differ from another's.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree can be hollow inside.
pages.brief: A cluster of broad green leaves in the foreground, with an old tree behind it. The tree trunk is thick and hollow inside, open like a dark cave in the wood. The leaves hang from a branch near the hollow opening.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree has a sharp trunk.
pages.brief: A spray of narrow green leaves in front of a tree trunk covered in sharp, pointed spikes. The trunk rises straight up in a forest, and the leaves hang close to the spiky bark. The sharp points stand out clearly on the trunk.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree makes sweet syrup.
pages.brief: A cluster of lobed green leaves in front of a tree trunk. Golden sweet syrup runs down the bark in slow drips, shining in the light. The tree stands in a green forest, and the leaves are broad and clear.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree has many colors.
pages.brief: Several leaves in red, orange, yellow and green in the foreground, with a tree behind them covered in the same many-colored leaves. The tree stands in an autumn woodland, and the fallen leaves around it show many colors.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree looks like an umbrella.
pages.brief: A spread of small green leaves in front of a tree whose branches fan out wide and flat, like an open umbrella. The tree stands alone in a grassy place, and its leafy top forms a broad, rounded canopy above the trunk.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree is the tallest.
pages.brief: A close bunch of green leaves in the foreground, with an extremely tall tree rising behind them. The tree's trunk goes up and up into the sky, far above the other trees, and its top is lost in the high branches.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree is covered in fruit.
pages.brief: Round green leaves in the foreground, and behind them a tree loaded with bright fruit among its branches. The fruit hangs heavy on the tree, and the leafy canopy is full of it. The tree stands in a sunny place with grass below.

pages.text: See these leaves? Their tree grows roots from branches.
pages.brief: A cluster of glossy green leaves in the foreground, with a wide tree behind them. Thick roots hang down from its branches and reach toward the ground, making new supports. The tree stands in a warm, humid forest with tangled wood.

pages.text: All trees have their own special leaves. All leaves have their own special trees!
pages.brief: A wide view of many different trees standing together in a green landscape, each with its own leaves. In the foreground, a mixed pile of leaves shows different shapes and colors. The trees and leaves fill the scene, showing many special kinds side by side.

books.title: All About Orcas
books.art_why: Orcas are real animals living in the ocean today, so real photographs work best.

pages.text: Orcas are mammals. They are big dolphins.
pages.brief: A large orca swims through open blue ocean water, its smooth black body and white markings clearly visible from the side. Behind and beside it, a second orca glides nearby, showing that these animals live and travel together as a family group of big dolphins.

pages.text: Orcas live in the ocean. They live in cold water.
pages.brief: Two orcas surface in cold, grey-green ocean water, their backs breaking the ripples. Around them the sea stretches wide and choppy under a pale sky, with small waves and a hint of icy shoreline in the far distance, showing the cold water where these animals make their home.

pages.text: Orcas breathe air. They breathe through a blowhole.
pages.brief: An orca floats at the surface of the sea, its head lifted, while a misty spray of breath puffs up from the blowhole on top of its head. Ripples spread around the black and white body as the animal takes in air above the water.

pages.text: Orcas are black and white. Their color helps them hide in the water.
pages.brief: A single orca swims close to the surface, showing its strong black back, white belly and white eye patch. The dark water around it blends with the black parts of its body, while sunlight and shadow play over the surface, showing how the colors help it hide.

pages.text: Orcas are called “killer whales.” They are strong hunters.
pages.brief: A powerful orca surges forward through the sea, mouth slightly open and body leaning into the chase, water swirling around its fins. Its black and white shape looks strong and fast as it hunts in the open ocean under a bright, cold sky.

pages.text: Orcas are also called “wolves of the sea.” They hunt in packs.
pages.brief: Three orcas swim close together in a line, moving through dark ocean water as a group. Their fins cut the surface and their bodies stay near one another, showing how these animals hunt together in packs rather than alone.

pages.text: Orcas have big teeth. They do not chew their food.
pages.brief: A close view of an orca's head at the surface, mouth open to show a row of big, sharp teeth. The animal holds a fish in its jaws without chewing, the silvery fish whole and shining against the dark water and the whale's white chin.

pages.text: Orcas eat other sea animals. They hunt fish, seals, and even other dolphins.
pages.brief: An orca hunts in cold sea water, chasing a leaping silver fish while a seal swims nearby and another dolphin moves in the distance. The black and white hunter turns through the water, showing the sea animals it feeds on.

pages.text: Orcas have big fins. Fins help them move through the water.
pages.brief: An orca swims steadily forward, its large dorsal fin standing tall above the water and its side flippers sweeping out. White water streams past the fins as the animal pushes through the ocean, moving fast and smooth under a grey sky.

pages.text: Orcas are powerful ocean animals.
pages.brief: A strong orca rises near the surface of the sea, black body gleaming and white markings bright, with wide ocean all around it. Its tall fin and powerful shape fill the picture, showing a mighty animal at home in the open water.

books.title: Food Trucks
books.art_why: Food trucks, cooks and the food they sell all exist today and photograph well.

pages.text: Food trucks are trucks where people make and sell food.
pages.brief: A bright food truck parked at the kerb of a sunny street, its side hatch open. Inside, two people in aprons cook and serve at the counter while a customer stands at the window buying food and two more people wait behind on the pavement.

pages.text: Each food truck has a kitchen inside.
pages.brief: A view inside one food truck showing the small kitchen: a cook at a stove with pans, a fridge, shelves of supplies, and a little counter by the open serving window where a plate of food is passed out to a waiting customer.

pages.text: This food truck sells fish and chips. This food truck sells barbecue.
pages.brief: Two food trucks parked side by side. On the first, a cook lifts a basket of golden fish and chips from the fryer; on the second, a barbecue grill smokes while a cook turns meat over the coals with long tongs.

pages.text: This food truck sells chicken. This food truck sells pizza.
pages.brief: Two more food trucks, one beside the other. The first has trays of cooked chicken on its counter with a cook serving portions; the second shows a pizza being slid from a hot oven onto a board.

pages.text: This food truck sells Indian food. This food truck sells Japanese food.
pages.brief: Two food trucks together. One counter holds small bowls of Indian food with a cook ladling out a portion; the next truck shows Japanese food arranged in boxes and a cook placing pieces inside with chopsticks.

pages.text: This food truck sells hot dogs. This food truck sells grilled cheese sandwiches.
pages.brief: A food truck counter with hot dogs lined up in soft rolls, a cook adding sauce from a bottle. Beside it, another truck shows grilled cheese sandwiches cooking on a hot plate, one being flipped with a spatula.

pages.text: This food truck sells seafood. This food truck sells tacos.
pages.brief: Two food trucks parked near each other. One displays seafood on ice with a cook lifting a portion out; the other has tacos filled and folded on the counter, a cook handing one to a customer at the window.

pages.text: This food truck sells ribs. This food truck sells hamburgers.
pages.brief: Two final food trucks side by side. One shows racks of ribs being brushed with sauce by a cook; the other has hamburgers sizzling on a grill, a cook pressing a bun down on a patty.

pages.text: Food trucks go wherever there are crowds of people.
pages.brief: A food truck parked in a busy park where a large crowd of people has gathered. Families sit on the grass, a queue waits at the open window, and people walk past holding food, the truck parked right among them.

pages.text: The food can taste really good!
pages.brief: A close view of a person biting into food just bought at a food truck, smiling happily. Behind them the open window shows a cook handing another portion out to a customer, with more food hot on the counter.

books.title: Goodbye Snow
books.art_why: Snow, shovels, plows and dump trucks are real things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Some places get a lot of snow.
pages.brief: A wide view of a town after heavy snowfall: rooftops, fences and parked cars buried under thick white snow, snow banked high along the street edges, flakes still falling, and no bare ground or pavement anywhere in sight.

pages.text: When snow gets in the way, it must be removed. There are many ways to remove snow.
pages.brief: A snowy street where deep snow has piled up across a doorway and along the sidewalk, blocking the way, with drifted snow heaped against walls and steps, showing how much snow has to be cleared before anyone can get through.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a shovel.
pages.brief: A person in a winter coat, hat and gloves stands on a snowy sidewalk pushing a wide-bladed shovel, lifting a load of snow off the pavement and tossing it onto a growing pile beside the path.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a brush.
pages.brief: A person in winter clothing holds a stiff hand brush and sweeps snow off a car, brushing the white powder from the roof and windows so it falls away onto the snowy ground below.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snowblower.
pages.brief: A person in a heavy coat pushes a snowblower along a snowy driveway, the machine's blades scooping up snow and throwing a high white arc of it out through the chute onto the lawn.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snowplow.
pages.brief: A large truck with a wide angled plow blade on its front drives along a snow-covered road, pushing a long curl of snow ahead of the blade and leaving dark cleared pavement behind it.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with salt.
pages.brief: Close view of a snowy, icy sidewalk with grainy salt scattered across the surface, and a gloved hand tipping more salt from a scoop so the grains spread over the frozen ground.

pages.text: Snow can be removed with a snow melter.
pages.brief: A snow melter machine sits on a snowy street, its open top filled with shovelled snow, warm steam rising from the machine as the snow inside melts down into water.

pages.text: Dump trucks may take snow away.
pages.brief: A dump truck on a snowy street with its bed tilted up, snow being loaded into the back by a machine, the truck waiting to carry the piled snow away from the road.

pages.text: Where does a dump truck take snow? A snow dump!
pages.brief: A huge open snow dump site where dump trucks tip out loads of snow, forming enormous white mounds and piles that stretch across the clearing in the winter landscape.

books.title: Alive with Light
books.art_why: Bioluminescent animals and plants exist today and can be photographed in the real world.

pages.text: Light helps animals see the world around them. It’s hard to see things where there is not much light.
pages.brief: A dim forest floor at dusk where a few shapes are barely visible in the shadows, while a brighter patch of daylight shows small animals clearly. The contrast shows how light helps animals see the world around them.

pages.text: Some living things can make light on their own.
pages.brief: A dark underwater scene where a single small creature glows softly against the black water, its own light shining from its body with no lamp or sun nearby, showing a living thing making light by itself.

pages.text: Some living things make blue light.
pages.brief: Close view of tiny living things in dark water giving off a soft blue glow, several small points of blue light scattered across the black background and drifting slowly through the water.

pages.text: Some living things make yellow light.
pages.brief: A dark scene with small living things shining yellow, warm golden light coming from their bodies as they sit on a leaf and in the shadows around them.

pages.text: Some living things make red light.
pages.brief: Living things glowing red in a dim place, deep red light coming from their small bodies while everything else around them stays dark and hard to see.

pages.text: Living things can make green light, too.
pages.brief: Small living things giving off green light in darkness, a few soft green glows spread across damp ground and low plants, lighting up the space right around them.

pages.text: The light can help living things catch their food.
pages.brief: A glowing creature in dark water or dim air with light shining from its body toward a smaller animal nearby, the light helping it catch its food.

pages.text: The light can help living things find their mates.
pages.brief: Two glowing living things facing each other in the dark, each making its own light, the glow passing between them as they find each other.

pages.text: The light can help protect living things so they stay safe.
pages.brief: A glowing living thing in a dark place with a larger animal nearby, the sudden bright flash of light making the bigger animal turn away and leave it safe.

pages.text: People don’t have bodies that give off light. People can enjoy seeing other things alive with light!
pages.brief: People standing outdoors at night, looking at glowing living things around them, their faces lit by the soft light while they watch and enjoy the sight.

books.title: City Places
books.art_why: City places such as parks, stores, zoos and stadiums exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: There are many places in the city. Let’s find out what some of them are.
pages.brief: A wide view of a busy city street with many kinds of places side by side — tall buildings, storefronts, trees and open ground — with people walking along the sidewalks and cars on the road, showing that a city holds many different places to visit.

pages.text: People come here to have fun. It is a park. What is this place?
pages.brief: A green city park on a sunny day. Children run across the grass, a family sits on a bench, and a dog trots beside them. Trees and a path curve through the park, and people are smiling and enjoying themselves in this open space.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a store. People come here to shop.
pages.brief: Inside a neighbourhood store, shelves are stacked with goods. Shoppers walk the aisles carrying baskets, a woman reaches for an item on a shelf, and a cashier stands at the counter near the front door where people come in to shop.

pages.text: People come here to see animals. It is a zoo. What is this place?
pages.brief: At the city zoo, families stand along a fence and look at the animals. An elephant stands in a grassy enclosure behind a low wall, and children point and watch. Trees and rocks fill the animal area while visitors stroll past on the path.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a skyscraper. Office workers come here to work.
pages.brief: A tall glass skyscraper rises above the city streets. Office workers in neat clothes walk through the front entrance carrying bags and cups of coffee, while others look out from the many windows high above the busy sidewalk below.

pages.text: Players come here to play ball. It is a stadium. What is this place?
pages.brief: Inside a large stadium, players in team colours run across the field chasing a ball. Crowds fill the seats around the field, and goalposts stand at each end. The players are in the middle of the game, playing ball in front of the spectators.

pages.text: What is this place? It is a parking garage. People come here to park their cars.
pages.brief: A concrete parking garage with several levels. Cars are parked neatly in painted spaces, a driver steps out of an open car door, and a ramp leads up to the next level where more cars sit parked in rows.

pages.text: What do you do in the city? in many places in the city. People do many different things.
pages.brief: People doing many different things in many places in the city: a woman shops with a bag, a child plays in a park, a worker enters an office building, and a family walks toward a stadium. Streets and buildings fill the background behind them.

books.title: All Kinds of Farms
books.art_why: Farms, farm animals, crops, and foods exist in the real world today.

pages.text: What Lives on Farms? Cows live on farms. Milk comes from cows. People drink milk.
pages.brief: On a farm, several cows stand in a grassy field near a fence. A person drinks milk, and milk is shown beside the cows, making it clear that milk comes from cows and people drink milk.

pages.text: People make cheese and butter from milk.
pages.brief: In a kitchen, people make cheese and butter from milk. Milk sits on a worktable beside cheese and butter, and the people's hands are busy as they work. The scene focuses on the milk and the foods made from it.

pages.text: Sheep live on farms. Wool comes from sheep. People make clothes from wool.
pages.brief: On a farm, sheep stand in a grassy field with thick wool. Nearby, people make clothes from wool, and clothing made from wool is shown, connecting the sheep and their wool to clothes people wear.

pages.text: Chickens live on farms. Eggs come from chickens. People eat eggs for breakfast.
pages.brief: On a farm, chickens move around a yard. Eggs from the chickens are shown nearby, and a person eats eggs for breakfast at a table, connecting the chickens and their eggs to a breakfast meal.

pages.text: What Grows on Farms? Apples grow on farms. People eat apples.
pages.brief: On a farm, apple trees grow in an orchard. Apples are shown on the trees, and a person eats an apple nearby, showing that apples grow on farms and people eat apples. The scene is simple and clear.

pages.text: Other fruits grow on farms, too. People eat fruits.
pages.brief: On a farm, other fruit plants grow in rows. Several kinds of fruit are shown among the plants, and people eat fruits nearby, showing that other fruits grow on farms too and people eat fruits.

pages.text: Sugarcane grows on farms. Sugar comes from sugarcane. Sugar makes foods sweet.
pages.brief: On a farm, sugarcane plants grow tall in a field. Sugar from the sugarcane is shown nearby, and sweet foods are shown to make it clear that sugar comes from sugarcane and makes foods sweet.

pages.text: Cotton grows on farms. People use cotton to make clothing. Shirts, pants, and socks are made from cotton.
pages.brief: On a farm, cotton plants grow in a field. Cotton from the plants is shown, and people use cotton to make clothing; a shirt, pants, and socks made from cotton are shown nearby. The clothing is simple and clear.

pages.text: What did you use today that came from a farm?
pages.brief: A wide farm landscape with fields stretches across the scene, with open space and a calm view. No specific product is singled out, leaving room to think about what was used today that came from a farm.

books.title: The Four Seasons
books.art_why: The seasons and outdoor scenes exist in the real world and can be photographed.

pages.text: There are four seasons.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor landscape is shown as four separate seasonal views of the same setting, placed side by side. One view suggests a new season, one is bright and warm, one shows changing trees, and one is cold and snowy. No people appear. The open sky and land make the four seasons easy to compare.

pages.text: In spring, the rain falls. Children play in the puddles.
pages.brief: Rain falls steadily over an outdoor scene. Several children splash and play in shallow puddles on the ground, laughing as they move through the water. Wet surfaces reflect the gray sky. The children stay outdoors in the spring rain.

pages.text: The days get longer. Summer comes.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor view shows the sky staying bright late in the day, with the sun low and the daylight lasting longer. Green plants and open ground are visible. The scene feels warmer as summer arrives, with no people present. The emphasis is on the lengthening day and the coming summer.

pages.text: In summer, the days are hot. Children play at the beach.
pages.brief: Bright hot sun shines over a sandy beach beside calm water. Several children play at the beach, running near the water and digging in the sand. The sky is clear and the day looks very warm. The children enjoy summer at the beach.

pages.text: It starts to cool off. Fall comes.
pages.brief: An outdoor landscape begins to cool. The light looks softer, a cool breeze moves through the plants, and the air no longer feels hot. Trees and ground are shown in an open natural setting. No people appear. The scene marks the change from summer toward fall.

pages.text: In fall, trees lose their leaves. Children make faces on pumpkins.
pages.brief: Trees stand with many leaves falling to the ground in an outdoor fall scene. Nearby, children sit or stand around pumpkins and make faces on them, concentrating on their pumpkins. Fallen leaves cover the ground around the trees. The children are busy with the pumpkins as autumn continues.

pages.text: The winds get colder. Winter comes.
pages.brief: Cold wind blows across an outdoor landscape. Trees and plants bend slightly as the wind moves through, and the air looks gray and chilly. The ground is bare and the sky is overcast. No people appear. The scene shows the colder winds bringing winter closer.

pages.text: In winter, the days are shorter. Children play in the snow.
pages.brief: Snow covers an outdoor landscape under a short, dim winter day. Several children play in the snow, moving about and enjoying the cold weather. Bare trees stand in the background, and the sky looks pale. The children are active in the snowy scene.

pages.text: The snow melts. It gets warmer. Spring comes again.
pages.brief: Snow is melting across an outdoor landscape as the air grows warmer. Patches of ground appear through the shrinking snow, and water runs in small streams. Plants begin to show fresh growth, and the sky looks brighter. No people appear. The scene shows spring returning after winter.

pages.text: Children have fun in all seasons!
pages.brief: Children have fun outdoors in all four seasons. The scene brings together children enjoying spring rain, a hot summer beach, fall pumpkins, and winter snow in separate views. Each group of children is active and happy in its own seasonal setting. The four seasons are shown together.

books.title: Shapes in Tide Pools
books.art_why: Tide pools, starfish, crabs, snails and mussels all exist today and can be photographed on rocky shores.

pages.text: There are pools of water on rocky shores. They are called tide pools.
pages.brief: A rocky shoreline at low tide, with several shallow pools of clear water held between dark, uneven rocks. Small ripples and wet stone edges show where the sea has pulled back, leaving the pools standing on the shore.

pages.text: Many animals live in tide pools.
pages.brief: A close view into one tide pool on the rocky shore, where many small sea animals are gathered. Some cling to the rock walls, others rest on the sandy bottom or among bits of weed, all living together in the shallow water.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has five arms. It is shaped like a star.
pages.brief: An animal with five arms spread out from a central middle, its body forming a star shape, rests in a shallow tide pool. Each arm tapers to a point, and the animal lies against the wet rock beneath the water.

pages.text: It is a starfish!
pages.brief: A starfish is shown clearly in the tide pool water, its five arms stretched outward in a star shape. It rests on the rocky bottom of the pool, its textured surface visible through the shallow, clear water.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has eight legs and two claws. Its body is shaped like an oval.
pages.brief: An animal with eight legs and two claws stands in a tide pool, its body shaped like an oval. The legs spread out around it, and the two claws are held forward near the rocky edge of the water.

pages.text: It is a crab!
pages.brief: A crab is shown in the tide pool, its oval body and eight legs clear, with two claws raised in front. It stands on the rocky bottom, partly in the shallow water, beside the pool wall.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal has one foot. It has a shell shaped like a triangle.
pages.brief: An animal with a single foot and a shell shaped like a triangle clings to the wet rock inside a tide pool. Its foot holds the rock while the pointed shell sits above it, close to the water's edge.

pages.text: It is a snail!
pages.brief: A snail is shown on the rocky shore in a tide pool, its triangular shell resting above the single foot that grips the wet stone. It sits at the edge of the shallow water among the rocks.

pages.text: Can you name this animal? This animal lives in a group. It has a shell shaped like an oval.
pages.brief: A group of animals with oval-shaped shells sits together on the rocks in a tide pool. Their oval shells are packed side by side, clinging to the wet stone where the shallow water covers them.

pages.text: It is a mussel!
pages.brief: A mussel is shown in the tide pool, its oval shell closed and resting against the rocky surface. It sits among the wet stones with shallow water around it, close to other oval shells.

books.title: Places Plants and Animals Live
books.art_why: Real habitats and wildlife that exist today are best shown in photographs.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the deserts. Deserts are very dry. Deserts can be very hot.
pages.brief: A wide desert of rippled sand dunes stretches under a bright, hot sun. The ground in front is dry and cracked. A small lizard stands on a flat rock, a spiny desert plant grows from the sand beside it, and a beetle walks between the stones. Nothing looks green or damp.

pages.text: Ocean water is very salty. Plants and animals live in the oceans.
pages.brief: Deep blue ocean water fills the scene, with sunlight slanting down through the surface. A group of small fish swims past clumps of green seaweed swaying in the water. Crabs move along the sandy sea floor below, and a few tiny plants grow on the rocks.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the mountains. Mountains are very tall and steep.
pages.brief: Tall, steep mountain slopes rise into rocky peaks, with patches of snow near the top. Small plants grow low in the cracks between rocks. A mountain goat stands firmly on a narrow ledge, and a bird glides past the cliff face in the clear air.

pages.text: Plains are very grassy and flat. Plants and animals live in the plains.
pages.brief: A broad, flat plain of waving grass stretches to the horizon under a wide sky. Grasses and low flowering plants cover the ground. A herd of grazing animals stands among the grass, heads down, feeding, while a bird stands nearby on the open ground.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in rivers. River water is not salty.
pages.brief: A river flows between grassy banks, the water clear and moving over smooth stones. Green plants grow along the edges and lean over the water. Small fish swim in the shallows, and a frog sits on a wet rock at the river's edge.

pages.text: Rainforests are very wet. Plants and animals live in rainforests.
pages.brief: A dense rainforest, crowded with tall trees and broad green leaves. Water drips from the leaves and hangs in the air as mist. Bright flowers grow on the trunks, a colourful bird perches on a branch, and a small animal climbs a vine in the wet shade.

pages.text: Plants and animals live in the tundra. The tundra is very cold. The tundra has no trees.
pages.brief: A flat, cold tundra under a pale sky, with frozen ground and small patches of snow. No trees stand anywhere. Low mosses and tiny plants cling to the ground, and a thick-coated animal with curved horns walks slowly across the open land, breathing in the cold air.

pages.text: Plants and animals live all around the world.
pages.brief: The whole Earth seen from a distance, a round world of blue ocean and green and brown land under swirls of cloud. Across the land and sea, plants and animals of many kinds are scattered, some in forests, some on dry ground, some in water.

books.title: Shoes Men Wear
books.art_why: Modern shoes and the people wearing them exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Flip-flops are summer shoes. Men wear them to the beach.
pages.brief: A man stands on a sunny beach in a pair of flip-flops, his bare toes showing against the sand. Warm summer light falls on him, and gentle ocean waves roll in behind him along the wide, open shore.

pages.text: Sneakers are everyday shoes. Men wear them to the park.
pages.brief: A man wearing everyday sneakers walks along a path in a green park. Trees and grass fill the background, and he steps forward comfortably in his laced shoes, out for a normal day in the park.

pages.text: Cleats are sport shoes. Men wear them to play soccer.
pages.brief: A man in sport cleats runs across a grassy soccer field, one foot planted and ready to kick. A soccer ball sits on the grass near him, and the open field stretches out under a bright sky.

pages.text: Hiking boots are outdoor shoes. Men wear them in the woods.
pages.brief: A man wearing sturdy hiking boots walks along a dirt trail in the woods. Tall trees and undergrowth surround him, and his boots grip the uneven ground as he moves deeper into the forest.

pages.text: Work boots are tough shoes. Men wear them to work.
pages.brief: A man stands at his workplace wearing tough work boots. The boots look strong and scuffed, and he stands firmly on the ground in them, dressed for a day of hard work on the job.

pages.text: Winter boots are warm shoes. Men wear them in the snow.
pages.brief: A man wearing warm winter boots stands outdoors in the snow. He is bundled up against the cold, his boots sunk slightly into the white ground, with soft snow falling and settling all around him.

pages.text: Wingtips are dress shoes. Men wear them to a dance.
pages.brief: A man wearing shiny wingtips, a smart pair of dress shoes, stands at a dance. He is dressed up for the occasion, his polished shoes visible as he stands on the floor in the middle of the gathering.

pages.text: Slippers are soft shoes. Men wear them around the house to rest their feet after a busy day.
pages.brief: A man rests at home wearing soft slippers. He sits comfortably with his feet up, his feet relaxed inside the slippers after a busy day, quiet and calm in his own house.

books.title: Country Animals
books.art_why: All the animals and country settings are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Some people live in the country. Many kinds of animals live in the country, too.
pages.brief: A countryside scene with a few people standing in a rural outdoor setting, surrounded by many different country animals visible in the fields and trees. The people and animals share the same setting, showing that both live in the country.

pages.text: Deer live in the country. They eat twigs from trees.
pages.brief: A deer stands beside trees in the country, stretching up to eat twigs from the branches. The tree and the deer are shown clearly in a natural outdoor setting, matching the page’s focus on deer eating twigs from trees.

pages.text: Robins live in the country. They make nests in trees.
pages.brief: A robin sits in a tree in the country, building a nest among the branches. The small bird is shown working on its nest in the tree, in a natural outdoor setting that shows where robins live and make nests.

pages.text: Squirrels live in the country. They eat nuts from trees.
pages.brief: A squirrel clings to a tree in the country, holding and eating nuts from the branches. The tree and squirrel fill the outdoor scene, showing the squirrel’s food and the place where it lives.

pages.text: Geese and ducks live in the country. They swim in lakes.
pages.brief: Geese and ducks float and swim on a lake in the country. The birds are shown together on the water, with the lake and surrounding outdoor setting visible, matching the page’s focus on geese and ducks swimming in lakes.

pages.text: Raccoons live in the country. They wash their food in rivers.
pages.brief: Raccoons stand at the edge of a river in the country, washing their food in the water. Their paws and food are near the river, and the outdoor setting shows the river where the raccoons wash what they eat.

pages.text: Foxes live in the country. They run and play in fields.
pages.brief: Foxes run and play together in an open country field. The grassy field is shown around them, and the foxes are captured in motion, matching the page’s focus on foxes running and playing in fields outdoors.

pages.text: Cows live in the country. They eat grass from fields.
pages.brief: Cows stand in a country field, eating grass. The grassy field fills the outdoor scene around the cows, showing the place where they live and the food they eat, matching the page’s focus on cows eating grass from fields.

pages.text: Mice live in the country. They eat grains from fields.
pages.brief: Mice are shown in a country field, eating grains near them. The small mice gather by the grain in the grassy outdoor setting, matching the page’s focus on mice eating grains from fields around them.

pages.text: Do you see animals where you live? What kinds of animals do you see?
pages.brief: A view of a place where people live, with several kinds of animals visible nearby. The scene invites the viewer to notice what animals can be seen in their own area, matching the page’s question about animals where you live.
